chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Mechanics of Competitive Devaluation

lessons.title: Capital Flows, FPI Money, and the Impossible Trinity

body.text: Every constraint covered so far in this course, why the gold standard collapsed, why Brazil taxed foreign inflows, why the RBI won't announce a target rate, traces back to one framework: a country can have a fixed exchange rate, free capital movement, and independent monetary policy, but never all three at once.

markDefs.definition: The Mundell-Fleming proposition that a country can only simultaneously maintain two of the following three: a fixed exchange rate, free international capital movement, and an independent domestic monetary policy. Pursuing the third undermines whichever of the other two is weaker.

children.text: , also called the trilemma, is the single most useful framework in this entire course. It says a country gets to choose exactly two of three things: a fixed exchange rate, free movement of capital across its borders, and the ability to set its own interest rates independently of the rest of the world. Chase all three at once and the system breaks, usually through a currency crisis, capital controls slapped on in a hurry, or the exchange rate peg being abandoned.

body.caption: The Three Corners of the Trinity

cells: Fixed exchange rate + free capital flows
Independent monetary policy: domestic rates must track the anchor currency's
Hong Kong's USD currency board; individual Eurozone members inside the euro
Free capital flows + independent monetary policy
A fixed exchange rate: the currency must float and absorb the pressure instead
The United States, Japan, and India's own managed float
Fixed exchange rate + independent monetary policy
Free capital mobility: capital controls are needed to hold both the other two
China's managed peg, backed by extensive capital controls

body.title: Quick Check: Apply the Trinity
body.question: A country wants a fixed exchange rate, completely free movement of capital in and out, and the freedom to set its own interest rates independently to manage domestic inflation, all at the same time. What does the impossible trinity say about this plan?
options: It works fine as long as the central bank is credible enough
At most two of the three are achievable simultaneously, the third has to give
Only the fixed exchange rate matters, the other two are irrelevant to the outcome
This is achievable permanently as long as forex reserves are large enough
body.explanation: This is the trilemma in its purest form: exactly the three goals it says cannot all be held at once. If capital moves freely and the exchange rate is fixed, domestic interest rates get pulled toward the anchor currency's rates. Large reserves can delay the reckoning, as Chapter 2's RBI lesson showed, but they don't repeal the trade-off, they only buy time to manage it.

body.text: This is the framework hiding underneath the 1930s gold standard collapse from Chapter 1. The gold standard was fixed exchange rates plus free capital mobility, since gold itself moved freely across borders. The price of keeping both was exactly the corner the trinity predicts: no independent monetary policy. Britain, Japan and the US didn't leave gold on a whim, they left specifically to reclaim the interest rate freedom the gold standard had taken from them, which is precisely why Eichengreen's research found early leavers recovered faster. The trilemma explains the entire chapter, decades before the term existed.

children.text: The 2010 Currency War, Seen Through the Trinity

Chapter 1 covered the Fed's QE-driven carry trade wave into Brazil and other emerging markets without naming the underlying constraint. The US sat comfortably in the free-capital-flows-plus-independent-policy corner: a floating dollar absorbed the effect of near-zero rates set purely for domestic reasons. Brazil wanted something harder: an open capital account to attract investment, a stable real to protect exporters, and independent rate-setting to manage its own inflation, all three at once. The trinity says that combination cannot hold, and Brazil's actual choice, the IOF tax on foreign inflows, was a direct, if partial, sacrifice of free capital mobility to preserve the other two.

markDefs.definition: The degree to which a country allows money to be freely converted and moved in and out for capital account transactions such as investment, lending and borrowing, as opposed to only for trade in goods and services.

children.text: India does not sit cleanly in any one corner, and that is deliberate. It has

, not the fully open capital account of the US corner: FPI debt limits, external commercial borrowing rules and sectoral FDI caps all restrict how freely capital moves. It runs a managed float, not a hard peg like Hong Kong's or China's. And since 2016, when the RBI Act was amended to formally establish inflation targeting through the Monetary Policy Committee with a 4% target (within a 2 to 6% band), India has leaned harder into the independent monetary policy leg than it had in earlier decades.

In trilemma terms, India sits inside the triangle rather than at a corner: partial openness on capital flows, partial flexibility on the exchange rate, and meaningful but not unconstrained independence on rates. This costs India the clean efficiency of any single corner, but buys flexibility to lean toward whichever leg matters most in a given crisis, tightening capital flow rules during a taper-tantrum-style outflow, or leaning on the managed float to absorb a shock like the 2015 yuan devaluation, without ever being fully locked into one extreme.

stats.label: Capital account
stats.context: Open for most FDI and much FPI, restricted for debt inflows and external borrowing

stats.label: Exchange rate regime
stats.context: Market-determined since 1993, RBI smooths volatility without a target level

stats.label: Monetary policy framework
stats.context: 4% target within a 2 to 6% band, set by the Monetary Policy Committee

body.title: State the Trilemma
body.textWithBlank: According to the impossible trinity, a country can achieve at most ___ of the following three goals at once: a fixed exchange rate, free capital mobility, and independent monetary policy.
body.explanation: Two. Pursuing all three at once is what the framework says is structurally impossible, which is why every episode in this course eventually involves one of the three being sacrificed, sometimes suddenly and sometimes by deliberate, gradual policy design.

body.title: You Are Advising Indian Policymakers, Late 2010
body.scenario: The Fed's QE2 is pulling carry trade capital into Indian debt and equity markets, covered in Chapter 1. Policymakers want three things at once: continued capital account liberalisation to attract long-term FDI, a stable rupee to protect exporters from the appreciation this inflow is causing, and independent RBI interest rates to manage domestic inflation, which is already running hot.
body.prompt: Using the impossible trinity, explain why India cannot fully achieve all three goals here, and recommend which one to partially sacrifice, and how.
body.modelAnswer: All three cannot hold simultaneously once capital is flowing in at this scale. If India keeps the capital account fully open and also wants a stable rupee, it would need to match global (effectively Fed-driven) rate conditions, sacrificing the independent, inflation-focused rate policy it badly needs given hot domestic inflation. The workable answer is a partial sacrifice of free capital mobility, not a full retreat: use targeted, temporary speed bumps on the most speculative categories of inflow (similar in spirit to Brazil's IOF tax, though India in practice leaned more on FPI debt limits and sectoral caps than a blanket tax), while letting the rupee absorb some of the pressure through appreciation rather than defending a hard level, and keeping RBI rate policy focused on the domestic inflation mandate. This preserves meaningful capital account access and monetary independence, at the cost of a fully free capital account and a perfectly stable exchange rate, exactly the kind of middle-of-the-triangle compromise India has run since 1993 rather than committing to a single pure corner.

cards.definition: A country can hold at most two of: a fixed exchange rate, free capital mobility, and independent monetary policy.
How freely a country allows money to move in and out for investment, lending and borrowing, as opposed to trade transactions alone.
A country's choice to fully commit to two of the trilemma's three goals while completely sacrificing the third, such as Hong Kong's currency board or China's capital-controlled peg.
India's monetary policy framework since 2016, targeting 4% CPI inflation within a 2 to 6% band via the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee.

points: The impossible trinity says a country can hold at most two of: a fixed exchange rate, free capital mobility, and independent monetary policy.
The 1930s gold standard was the fixed-rate-plus-free-capital corner, and countries left it specifically to reclaim the monetary independence that corner had cost them.

The 2010 currency war era pitted the US's free-capital-plus-independent-policy corner against emerging markets trying to hold all three goals at once, forcing capital control responses like Brazil's IOF tax.
India occupies the middle of the triangle rather than a pure corner: partial capital account convertibility, a managed float, and inflation-targeted monetary independence since 2016.
This middle position trades away corner-solution efficiency for flexibility, letting India lean on whichever tool matters most in a given crisis rather than being locked into one extreme.

This closes Chapter 2's mechanics. Chapter 3 moves to full case studies, China's yuan management, Japan's carry trade, and how Indian markets actually react when these mechanics play out in real time.
